title: Grimacing Face Emoji 😬 Meaning: Yikes and Awkwardness
description: 😬 is the “yikes” face: clenched teeth for awkward moments, mistakes and nervous tension. Learn how to read it in texts and why it is often confused with 😁.
summary: 😬 shows a face with wide eyes and clenched, bared teeth. It means “yikes” or “eek.” People use it for awkward moments, mistakes they have just noticed, nervous anticipation and secondhand embarrassment. It is tension, not happiness, even though the teeth can look like a grin.
meaning: The expression is the one people make when they step on a creaky stair at midnight. 😬 covers every situation where the right word is “oops” or “yikes”: you sent the message to the wrong person, you forgot the birthday, you are about to deliver news someone will not like. It admits the awkwardness openly and hopes that doing so will soften the fallout.

It is just as useful for reacting to other people's situations. A friend describes a disastrous date or a tense family dinner, and 😬 replies “that sounds painful.” This is sympathy mixed with secondhand discomfort. It can also carry a note of judgment, as in a response to someone's questionable decision, where it means “oh no, you didn't.”

Nervousness is the third major use. Before an exam, an interview, a difficult conversation or a tight deadline, 😬 shows gritted teeth and a racing pulse. “Presentation in ten minutes 😬” is the feeling of bracing for impact. In this sense it sits between the mild worry of 😅 and the real distress of 😰.

A design quirk shaped how people read it. On older Apple systems, the beaming face 😁 was drawn with a tight row of teeth that looked a lot like a grimace, so a cheerful message could arrive looking pained, and the reverse. Apple later redrew 😁 to look clearly happy. The episode is a big reason people learned to check the eyes: 😬 has round, open ones, and no smile in them.

contexts.label: In texting
contexts.body: It cushions apologies and bad news: “so… I might be twenty minutes late 😬.” It is the natural reply when a friend recounts something cringeworthy. Sent alone after someone's bold statement, it suggests the sender thinks it was a mistake or that trouble is coming, without saying so outright.

contexts.label: At work
contexts.body: This is among the more office-friendly ways to acknowledge a slip, such as a missed attachment or a calendar mix-up. It shows you know it was awkward. Follow it with the fix, though. For errors with real consequences, a clear apology in words is better than a face that says “eek.”

contexts.label: On social media
contexts.body: Comment sections use it for cringe: awkward interviews, failed proposals, celebrity gaffes, and posts that aged badly. It is a mild alternative to piling on, expressing discomfort more than mockery. People caption their own embarrassing stories and nervous announcements with it as well.

contexts.label: From a crush
contexts.body: It rarely means anything romantic. They may be nervous about something they just said, apologizing for a late reply, or cringing at their own joke. If it follows your message, they might have found it awkward. A relaxed response that takes the pressure off is usually the best move.

Anxiously hoping something turns out fine.
Watching an uncomfortable scene unfold and feeling the tension.
Peak cringe; almost too awkward to keep looking.

confusedWith.difference: 😁 shows teeth in a broad grin with smiling, curved eyes and means real happiness. 😬 shows clenched teeth with round, uneasy eyes and means tension. They were easy to confuse on older designs, so look at the eyes, not the teeth.
😅 laughs with a drop of sweat and means relief or sheepishness after a close call. 😬 is still in the uncomfortable moment. 😅 says “phew, that was close”; 😬 says “uh-oh, this is happening.”

🫣 hides behind a hand and peeks, adding shyness or dread to the cringe. 😬 has nothing to hide behind and faces the awkwardness directly. Use 🫣 when you cannot bear to look and 😬 when you are gritting your teeth through it.

avoid: Do not use it as a smile; many people will read tension or disapproval where you meant cheer.
Avoid it as your full response to serious bad news, since “yikes” is too light for real hardship.
Skip it when commenting on someone's appearance or work unless you intend to say it makes you uncomfortable.
design: A yellow face with round, wide-open eyes and a rectangular mouth showing two rows of clenched teeth. There is no curve to the mouth, which separates it from grinning faces. Today's vendor designs agree closely. The earlier resemblance between this emoji and Apple's old beaming face has been resolved by redesigns that made the smile clearly a smile.

faqs.a: No. It is a grimace, showing clenched teeth from discomfort, nerves or embarrassment. People sometimes send it as a grin because of the visible teeth, but most recipients will read it as “yikes” or “awkward.”

faqs.q: What does 😬 mean from a girl or a guy?
faqs.a: That something feels awkward or nerve-racking to them. It might be about their own message, a situation they are describing, or occasionally your last text. It is not flirtatious and not hostile; it just flags discomfort.

faqs.q: What is the difference between 😬 and 😁?
faqs.a: 😁 is joy, with eyes curved in a smile. 😬 is tension, with eyes wide and round. Both show teeth, which caused a lot of confusion on older phones where the two drawings looked more alike than they do now.
Not usually. Clenched teeth can suggest anger in real life, but the emoji's wide eyes make it read as nervous or awkward. For anger, people use 😠, 😤 or 😡.

If they are apologizing or nervous, reassure them: “no worries” or “you'll be great.” If they are reacting to your story, they are sympathizing, so carry on. If it follows something you said, consider whether it landed awkwardly and lighten the tone.
